Let’s dive into Chapter 3: Edit Ruthlessly Without Losing Meaning.
Now that you’ve got a clear structure, it’s time to zoom in on your words. This is where the magic happens—where you make every single word pull its weight, and you cut out anything that doesn’t serve your core message.
A lot of people worry that being ruthless with editing will make their writing seem cold, or like something’s missing. But here’s the thing: when you carefully trim away the clutter, your message actually gets warmer and more engaging. There’s simply less to distract your reader, so what really matters stands out.
The trick is to keep the heart of your message intact, while letting go of anything that’s just taking up space.
Editing for brevity is a skill, and like any skill, it gets better the more you practice. Start by looking at each sentence and asking yourself, “Is this adding value? Is there a simpler way to say this? Can I take out a word or two without changing what I mean?” When you approach editing this way, it actually becomes pretty creative—not just a technical chore.
Here are a few simple guidelines for editing effectively:
First, ditch filler words. Phrases like “very,” “really,” or “in order to” usually don’t add much.
Next, swap out long-winded explanations for direct statements.
Try not to repeat yourself by saying the same thing in different ways.
Use active voice whenever you can—it makes your sentences clearer and more direct.
And, if you can use a simpler word instead of a complicated one, go for it.
Want an example? Instead of writing, “We are reaching out to you in order to inform you that the meeting has been rescheduled,” just say, “The meeting is rescheduled.” It’s the same message, but it’s delivered faster, and it’s a lot easier to understand.
But remember, editing isn’t just about cutting for the sake of cutting. You still want your message to feel friendly and respectful—not abrupt. Even when you’re being brief, a quick “hello” or a simple “thanks” can make all the difference in keeping your tone warm.
In a team setting, building a culture of editing can make everyone’s communication sharper and more productive. When colleagues help each other spot ways to tighten up their messages, it keeps everyone focused and efficient. Over time, this habit can totally change how organizations share information and make decisions.
So, what are some practical habits you can use to become a better editor?
Try reading your messages out loud—you’ll catch awkward phrasing or extra words right away.
If it’s important, ask a colleague to look over your message for clarity and brevity.
Set yourself a word or sentence limit for routine communications—it’s a great way to stay disciplined.
And don’t forget about digital tools or checklists. They’re great for spotting common sources of wordiness.
Editing isn’t about being perfect. It’s about getting a little better with each draft. Every time you revise, you get closer to the heart of your message. The end result? Messages that are not just shorter, but stronger and a whole lot more memorable.
Once you’ve got these editing skills down, you’re ready to take on the next challenge: using brevity across all kinds of digital communication. That’s where we’re headed next.
